course.subject: Science
course.map_objective: Explain how water moves around the Earth in a never-ending cycle, and what powers it.

units.name: Water goes up
units.objective: Describe how heat from the Sun turns liquid water into water vapour.

units.name: Water in the sky
units.objective: Explain how water vapour becomes clouds and falls back as rain or snow.

units.name: Water comes back
units.objective: Trace where water goes after it falls and how it returns to the sea.

ideas.title: Water cycle
ideas.objective: I can name the main stages of the water cycle in order.
ideas.explanation: The journey water takes as it moves between the sky, the land and the sea, over and over again.

ideas.title: Evaporation
ideas.objective: I can explain how the Sun’s heat turns liquid water into vapour.
ideas.explanation: When the Sun warms water in oceans, lakes and puddles, some of it turns into an invisible gas and rises into the air.

ideas.title: Condensation
ideas.objective: I can explain why water vapour turns back into drops when it cools.
ideas.explanation: As water vapour rises it cools down and turns back into tiny drops of liquid water.

ideas.title: Precipitation
ideas.objective: I can describe what makes water fall from clouds.
ideas.explanation: When cloud drops grow too heavy, they fall back to the ground.

ideas.title: Collection
ideas.objective: I can list places where fallen water gathers.
ideas.explanation: Water that falls gathers in oceans, rivers, lakes and underground, ready to start the cycle again.

ideas.title: Transpiration
ideas.objective: I can explain how plants put water back into the air.
ideas.explanation: Plants pull water up from their roots and let some of it escape from their leaves as vapour.

ideas.title: Freezing
ideas.objective: I can explain what happens to water when it freezes.
ideas.explanation: When water gets cold enough it turns into solid ice.

ideas.title: The Sun
ideas.objective: I can explain why the Sun is the engine of the water cycle.
ideas.explanation: The Sun gives off heat and light. Its energy is what keeps the water cycle moving.

ideas.title: Temperature
ideas.objective: I can describe how warming and cooling change water.
ideas.explanation: How hot or cold something is. Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.

ideas.title: Climate
ideas.objective: I can explain how climate affects rain and snow in a place.
ideas.explanation: The usual weather of a place over many years. It changes how much rain and snow falls.

ideas.title: Water vapour
ideas.objective: I can describe water vapour and where it comes from.
ideas.explanation: Water in the form of a gas. You cannot see it, but it is all around you in the air.

ideas.title: Clouds
ideas.objective: I can explain what clouds are made of.
ideas.explanation: Millions of tiny water drops or ice crystals floating together in the sky.

ideas.title: Rain & snow
ideas.objective: I can tell the difference between rain and snow.
ideas.explanation: The forms precipitation takes. Snow forms when the air is cold enough to freeze the drops.

ideas.title: Oceans
ideas.objective: I can explain why oceans matter to the water cycle.
ideas.explanation: Huge bodies of salt water that cover most of the Earth and hold most of its water.

ideas.title: Rivers
ideas.objective: I can trace how rivers carry water back to the sea.
ideas.explanation: Flowing fresh water that carries rain and melted snow from the land back to the sea.

ideas.title: Plants
ideas.objective: I can explain how plants take in and give back water.
ideas.explanation: Living things that drink water through their roots and return some of it to the air.

ideas.title: Glaciers
ideas.objective: I can explain how glaciers store and release water.
ideas.explanation: Giant, slow rivers of ice that store fresh water for hundreds of years.

ideas.title: Groundwater
ideas.objective: I can describe how water is stored underground.
ideas.explanation: Water that soaks into the soil and is stored between rocks underground.

categories.description: What causes or drives a change

assessment.question: What does the Sun have to do with water going up into the air?
key_points: The Sun gives heat/energy
that heat makes water evaporate

assessment.question: What changes when water gets warmer?
key_points: Warmer water evaporates faster
warm air can hold more water vapour

assessment.question: What is evaporation? Can you give me an example?
key_points: Liquid water turns into a gas (vapour) when heated
e.g. a puddle drying up

assessment.question: If water vapour is all around us, why can't I see it?
key_points: Water vapour is a gas and which is invisible

assessment.question: Where does most of the water that evaporates come from?
key_points: Mostly from the oceans and which hold most of Earth's water

assessment.question: How do plants get water, and what happens to some of it?
key_points: Roots take in water
some escapes from the leaves into the air

assessment.question: What is transpiration, and how is it like evaporation?
key_points: Plants release water vapour from leaves
both put water vapour into the air

assessment.question: Why does water vapour turn back into drops?
key_points: When vapour cools and it changes from gas back to liquid drops

assessment.question: What are clouds actually made of?
key_points: Tiny water drops or ice crystals and formed by condensation

assessment.question: Why does water fall out of clouds?
key_points: Drops join and grow too heavy to float and so they fall

assessment.question: When does it snow instead of rain?
key_points: When the air is cold enough to freeze the drops

assessment.question: Why do some places get much more rain than others?
key_points: Climate and the usual weather of a place over many years and shapes how much rain or snow falls

assessment.question: Where does water go after it falls?
key_points: It gathers in oceans and rivers and lakes and underground

assessment.question: How do rivers help water get back to the sea?
key_points: Rivers carry rain and melted snow downhill into the ocean

assessment.question: What is groundwater?
key_points: Water that soaks into the soil and is stored between rocks underground

assessment.question: What happens to water when it freezes?
key_points: When it gets cold enough it turns into solid ice

assessment.question: How can a glacier store water for a long time and then give it back?
key_points: Ice builds up over years
it melts slowly into rivers

assessment.question: Can you walk me through the whole water cycle, step by step?
key_points: Evaporation and condensation and precipitation and collection and and it repeats

practice.question: Which puddle dries fastest?
choices: A shallow puddle in the sun
A deep puddle in the shade
A puddle on a cold night
practice.answer: A shallow puddle in the sun
practice.explanation: More heat and more surface area both speed up evaporation.
demo_steps: The fastest ones escape the surface
A wider surface lets more escape
So a shallow puddle in the sun dries first

practice.question: The graph shows how much water evaporates each hour at different temperatures (°C, mL). How many millilitres evaporate each hour at 30 °C?
practice.explanation: Read up from 30 °C on the graph to the point (30, 9): 9 mL each hour.

practice.exercise_title: How much vapour can air hold?
practice.question: The table shows the most water vapour, in grams, that 1 m³ of air can hold at each temperature. How many more grams can it hold at 30 °C than at 20 °C?
practice.explanation: 30 °C holds 30 g and 20 °C holds 17 g, so 30 − 17 = 13 g more.

practice.exercise_title: How much vapour can air hold?
practice.question: Warm, wet air rises and cools. What happens to the water vapour in it?
choices: It turns into ice at once
practice.explanation: Cooler air holds less vapour, so the extra vapour turns back into liquid droplets.

practice.question: Which process turns water vapour back into liquid droplets?
practice.explanation: Condensation is vapour cooling into liquid; evaporation is the reverse.
